Toleration Act
tol-er-ā'-shun akt
n. (the Toleration Act, 1689, which gave English Dissenters freedom of worship under licence)
Latin tolerare, to bear, endure.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Toleration Act of 1689, passed in the first year of William and Mary, granted to Protestant Dissenters who would take the oaths of allegiance and subscribe thirty-four of the Thirty-nine Articles the freedom to worship in licensed meeting-houses with unlocked doors, and exempted their ministers from the penalties of the Clarendon Code. It was a limited measure and was never called a grant of liberty by its framers: Roman Catholics and antitrinitarians were excluded, the Test and Corporation Acts still barred Dissenters from office and from the universities, and tithes to the parish church were still due. But it ended a quarter-century of criminal prosecution for worship, and within a few years hundreds of meeting-houses were licensed and built. The generation that had been fined, gaoled and driven five miles from home received it with a gratitude later ages have found excessive. They had prayed for exactly this: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), and they knew who had turned the king's heart (Pro 21:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines toleration as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, and a licence as authority given to do some act.

expand to see more

TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state; freedom from penalty.

LI'CENSE, n. Authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.

DISSENT'ER, n. One who separates from the service and worship of the established church.

Key Scripture

1Ti 2:2 — "For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

Pro 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Mic 4:4 — "But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it."

Act 9:31 — "Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied."

Modern Corruption

The 1689 Act that ended criminal prosecution of Dissenting worship in England.

expand to see more

Toleration has since become a word for the proposition that all religious claims are equally valid, and so a church is now expected to purchase its liberty by professing that its own doctrine is one opinion among many. The Act of 1689 did nothing of the kind. It required subscription to thirty-four Articles and excluded those who denied the Trinity; it tolerated worship, not indifference.

The principle to recover is what such liberty is for: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2). The rest that the early churches had was spent being edified and multiplied (Act 9:31), and the picture Micah gives — “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid” (Mic 4:4) — is a mercy to be used, not a verdict on truth.

Usage

"“that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2) — what 1689 granted."

"“The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1) — how the Dissenters read it."

"“Then had the churches rest” (Act 9:31) — the licensed meeting-houses."
